items.statement:
Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system of finite type with $S$ finite and length function $\ell$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[def-cg-coxeter-diagram-components-and-finite-type]]), with canonical reflection representation $\rho:W\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$ on $V=\mathbb R^S$, Coxeter form $B$, root system $\Phi$ and reflection set $T=\{wsw^{-1}:w\in W,\ s\in S\}$ ([[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]], [[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]]). Since $W$ is finite, $B$ is positive definite ([[thm-cg-finite-type-positive-definite-criterion]]), so $(V,B)$ is a real inner product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), and $\rho(w)$ preserves $B$ for every $w\in W$ ([[lem-cg-reflection-representation-descends-and-root-norms]] (2)). Write $\mathrm O(V)$ for the group of $B$-preserving invertible linear maps $V\to V$ ([[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]]).

**(1) Reflection length.** For $w\in W$ put

$$\ell_T(w):=\min\{k\in\mathbb N:\ \text{there are }t_1,\dots,t_k\in T\text{ with }w=t_1t_2\cdots t_k\},$$

where the empty product ($k=0$) is the identity. The minimum exists because $S\subseteq T$ and $S$ generates $W$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]), so the admitted $k$ form a nonempty subset of $\mathbb N$, which has a least element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]).

**(2) Absolute order.** For $u,v\in W$ define $u\le_T v$ if and only if

$$\ell_T(v)=\ell_T(u)+\ell_T(u^{-1}v).$$

**(3) Moved and fixed spaces.** For a linear map $A:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) define the **moved space** and the **fixed space**

$$M(A):=\operatorname{im}(A-\mathrm{id}_V),\qquad F(A):=\ker(A-\mathrm{id}_V)$$

([[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]). For $A,B\in\mathrm O(V)$ define the relation $B\le_{\mathrm O}A$ if and only if

$$\dim M(A)=\dim M(B)+\dim M(B^{-1}A).$$

**(4) Conventions and abstentions.** For $u\in W$ write $M(u):=M(\rho(u))$ and $F(u):=F(\rho(u))$. This definition asserts no property of $\le_T$ and $\le_{\mathrm O}$ beyond the displayed formulas: it asserts neither that either relation is a partial order, nor that $\ell_T(w)=\dim M(w)$, nor that $B\le_{\mathrm O}A$ means that a shortest reflection factorization of $B$ is a prefix of one of $A$. Those properties are proved in [[thm-cg-carter-reflection-length-and-absolute-order]], the recorded justifier of this definition, and by the restriction and factorization lemmas of this page. No Choice is used: $S$, $W$, $\Phi$ and $T$ are finite and every object is finite-dimensional or set-theoretic.
items.strategy: A definitions-and-conventions item. **Reflection length.** $T$ is the set of conjugate simple reflections defined in [[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]]; since $s=1s1^{-1}$ one has $S\subseteq T$, and since $S$ generates $W$ every $w\in W$ is a product of elements of $T$, so the admitted $k$ form a nonempty subset of $\mathbb N$ with a least element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]); the empty product is the identity, so $\ell_T(1)=0$. No Choice is used: the minimum is taken in a well-ordered set of naturals, and no factorization is selected. **Absolute order.** $u\le_T v$ is recorded as a relation defined by the length-additivity formula; nothing is claimed about it here. **Moved and fixed spaces.** $M(A)$ and $F(A)$ are defined for an arbitrary linear map, with no orthogonality or invertibility used in the definition. **The orthogonal-order relation** is defined by the dimension formula, so that no existence of a reflection factorization of an orthogonal operator is presupposed; the rank-length equality and the prefix description are proved in the restriction lemma of this page. **Abstentions.** Clause (4) records exactly the properties that the later items prove before they are consumed, in the style of the earlier real-forms and arrangement definitions; the recorded justifier is [[thm-cg-carter-reflection-length-and-absolute-order]], and the restriction and factorization lemmas of this page are the further consumers of this definition. **Finite type.** Positive definiteness of $B$ is used only to make $(V,B)$ an inner product space and to license orthogonal projections; the identification $V\cong V^*$ of the arrangement page is not used in this definition.
items.proof_strategy: definition of reflection length, absolute order, and moved and fixed spaces, with the orthogonal-order relation defined by the dimension formula so that no factorization existence is presupposed

items.statement:
Let $(V,B)$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); on this page $V=\mathbb R^S$ with the positive definite Coxeter form $B$ of a Coxeter system of finite type ([[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]], [[thm-cg-finite-type-positive-definite-criterion]]), and $\mathrm O(V)$ is the group of $B$-preserving invertible linear maps ([[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]]). Let $M$, $F$ and $\le_{\mathrm O}$ be as in [[def-cg-reflection-length-absolute-order-and-moved-space]]. Then:

**(1) Basic identities.** For every $A\in\mathrm O(V)$ one has $F(A)=F(A^{-1})$, $M(A)=M(A^{-1})$, $M(A)=F(A)^\perp$, $V=M(A)\oplus F(A)$, $A(M(A))=M(A)$, $A(F(A))=F(A)$, and $(A-\mathrm{id})|_{M(A)}:M(A)\to M(A)$ is a bijection ([[cor-double-orthogonal-complement-and-dimension]], [[thm-rank-nullity]]). For all $X,Y\in\mathrm O(V)$, $M(XY)\subseteq M(X)+X\,M(Y)$ and hence $\dim M(XY)\le\dim M(X)+\dim M(Y)$.

**(2) The Wall form.** For $A\in\mathrm O(V)$ put

$$\chi_A(u,v):=B\bigl((A-\mathrm{id})|_{M(A)}^{-1}u,\ v\bigr)\qquad(u,v\in M(A)).$$

Then $\chi_A$ is a bilinear form on $M(A)$ satisfying

$$\chi_A(u,v)+\chi_A(v,u)=-B(u,v)\qquad(u,v\in M(A));$$

in particular $\chi_A$ is nondegenerate and its symmetric part is $-\tfrac12B|_{M(A)}$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]], [[prop-adjoint-algebra]]).

**(3) Subspace restriction.** Let $A\in\mathrm O(V)$, let $U\subseteq M(A)$ be a subspace and let $\Pi_U:V\to U$ be the orthogonal projection ([[def-orthogonal-projection]], [[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]). There is a unique $H_U\in\operatorname{End}(U)$ with $B(H_Uu,v)=\chi_A(u,v)$ for all $u,v\in U$, and it satisfies $H_U+H_U^*=-\mathrm{id}_U$, so that $H_U$ is invertible. Define $A_U\in\mathrm O(V)$ by $A_Uu=u+H_U^{-1}u$ for $u\in U$ and $A_U=\mathrm{id}$ on $U^\perp$. Then $M(A_U)=U$ and

$$(A_U-\mathrm{id})|_U^{-1}=H_U,\qquad H_Uu=\Pi_U\bigl((A-\mathrm{id})|_{M(A)}\bigr)^{-1}u\ \ (u\in U).$$

An element $A\in\mathrm O(V)$ is a reflection (that is, $\dim M(A)=1$) if and only if $A=\mathrm{id}-2\Pi_L$ for the line $L=M(A)$; in particular every line $L\subseteq V$ is the moved space of exactly one reflection of $\mathrm O(V)$ ([[thm-finite-dimensional-isometry-characterisations]]).

**(4) The restriction theorem.** For every subspace $U\subseteq M(A)$ one has $A_U\le_{\mathrm O}A$, that is $\dim M(A)=\dim U+\dim M(A_U^{-1}A)$; and for $U\subseteq U'\subseteq M(A)$ one has $(A_{U'})_U=A_U$, hence $A_U\le_{\mathrm O}A_{U'}$. Conversely every $B\in\mathrm O(V)$ with $B\le_{\mathrm O}A$ satisfies $M(B)\subseteq M(A)$, $\chi_A|_{M(B)}=\chi_B$ and $B=A_{M(B)}$. Consequently the assignment $U\mapsto A_U$ is a bijection from the set of subspaces of $M(A)$ onto $\{B\in\mathrm O(V):B\le_{\mathrm O}A\}$, with inverse $B\mapsto M(B)$, and it is an order isomorphism for inclusion of subspaces and $\le_{\mathrm O}$.

**(5) Rank-length equality and prefixes.** Let $A\in\mathrm O(V)$ and let $r_1,\dots,r_k\in\mathrm O(V)$ be reflections with $A=r_1r_2\cdots r_k$. Then $k\ge\dim M(A)$, and $A$ is a product of exactly $\dim M(A)$ reflections. Moreover $B\le_{\mathrm O}A$ if and only if there are a shortest factorization $A=r_1\cdots r_m$ (so $m=\dim M(A)$) and an index $k$ with $B=r_1\cdots r_k$.
items.strategy:
A lemma of finite-dimensional real linear algebra; the Coxeter specialization enters only through the choice of $(V,B)$ and is not used, and $A_U$ need not lie in $ho(W)$ (the companion example of the $I_2(4)$ rotation exhibits restrictions outside $W$). *(1)* For nondegenerate $B$, $B((A-\mathrm{id})x,y)=B(x,(A^{-1}-\mathrm{id})y)$, so $y\perp M(A)$ iff $(A^{-1}-\mathrm{id})y=0$ iff $Ay=y$; hence $M(A)^\perp=F(A)$ and, in finite dimension, $M(A)=F(A)^\perp$ and $V=M(A)\oplus F(A)$ ([[cor-double-orthogonal-complement-and-dimension]]). $A$ commutes with $A-\mathrm{id}$, so it preserves both summands; $(A-\mathrm{id})|_{M(A)}$ has kernel $F(A)\cap M(A)=0$ and is therefore bijective by [[thm-rank-nullity]]. Subadditivity is the identity $XY-\mathrm{id}=(X-\mathrm{id})Y+(Y-\mathrm{id})$. *(2)* With $S_A:=(A-\mathrm{id})|_{M(A)}^{-1}$ one has $S_A+S_A^*=-\mathrm{id}$ on $M(A)$: from $A^{-1}-\mathrm{id}=-A^{-1}(A-\mathrm{id})$ follows $(A^{-1}-\mathrm{id})^{-1}=-(A-\mathrm{id})^{-1}A$ and $(A-\mathrm{id})^{-1}-(A-\mathrm{id})^{-1}A=(A-\mathrm{id})^{-1}(\mathrm{id}-A)=-\mathrm{id}$ (and $(A^{-1}-\mathrm{id})^{-1}=((A-\mathrm{id})^{-1})^*$, since adjoints invert); transposing gives the stated identity. *(3)* Define $H_U=\Pi_US_A|_U$ and its adjoint by compressing $S_A^*$; the pairing formula follows from orthogonal projection, and nondegeneracy of $B|_U$ gives uniqueness; $H_U+H_U^*=-\mathrm{id}_U$ is (2) restricted to $U$, and $B(H_Uv,v)=-	frac12B(v,v)
e0$ for $v
e0$ gives invertibility. Orthogonality of $A_U=\mathrm{id}+H_U^{-1}\Pi_U$ follows from the finite-dimensional isometry characterization ([[thm-finite-dimensional-isometry-characterisations]]): with $(H_U^{-1})^*=(H_U^*)^{-1}$ and $\Pi_U^*=\Pi_U$ the product $A_U^*A_U$ equals $\mathrm{id}+[H_U^{-1}+(H_U^*)^{-1}+(H_U^*)^{-1}H_U^{-1}]\Pi_U$, and the bracket vanishes exactly because $H_U+H_U^*=-\mathrm{id}_U$. $M(A_U)=U$ because $A_U-\mathrm{id}=H_U^{-1}\Pi_U$. For a line $L$ the operator $H_L$ is $1	imes1$ with $H_L+H_L^*=-1$, so $H_L=-	frac12$ and $A_L=\mathrm{id}-2\Pi_L$; conversely an orthogonal $A$ with $\dim M(A)=1$ fixes $M(A)^\perp$ pointwise and acts on the line $M(A)$ by a scalar of modulus one different from $1$, hence by $-1$. *(4) Rank additivity.* Write $x=m+f$ with $m\in M(A)$, $f\in F(A)$ (valid by (1)). The equation $Ax=A_Ux$ is equivalent to $(A-\mathrm{id})m=H_U^{-1}\Pi_Um$, i.e. to $m=S_AH_U^{-1}u$ where $u=\Pi_Um\in U$; the identity $\Pi_US_A\Pi_U=H_U$ makes this consistent, and the solutions are $S_AH_U^{-1}u+f$ with $u\in U$, $f\in F(A)$ arbitrary. Hence $\dim\ker(A-A_U)=\dim U+\dim F(A)$, so $\operatorname{rank}(A-A_U)=\dim M(A)-\dim U$; since $A_U^{-1}A-\mathrm{id}=A_U^{-1}(A-A_U)$, the images have equal dimension and $\dim M(A)=\dim U+\dim M(A_U^{-1}A)$. *(4) Transitivity* follows by composing the displayed formula of (3) with $\Pi_U\Pi_{U'}=\Pi_U$ for $U\subseteq U'$, using $M(A_{U'})=U'$. *(4) Uniqueness.* Let $B\le_{\mathrm O}A$ and $C:=B^{-1}A$. From $A-\mathrm{id}=(B-\mathrm{id})C+(C-\mathrm{id})$ one gets $M(A)\subseteq M(B)+M(C)$ with $\dim M(A)=\dim M(B)+\dim M(C)$, hence $M(A)=M(B)\oplus M(C)$ and $M(B)\subseteq M(A)$. For $u\in U:=M(B)$ write $S_Au=x+y$ with $x\in U$, $y\in M(C)$ and apply $A-\mathrm{id}$: comparing the two direct summands gives $(C-\mathrm{id})(x+y)=0$ and $u=(B-\mathrm{id})(x+y)$, so $x+y-S_Bu\in F(B)=M(B)^\perp=U^\perp$ and $B(S_Au,v)=B(S_Bu,v)$ for all $v\in U$. Thus $\chi_A|_U=\chi_B$ and $\Pi_US_A\Pi_U=S_B$, and the formula of (3) gives $B=A_U$. The order isomorphism follows by applying the same statement to $A_{U'}$. *(5)* The lower bound is (1); for the upper bound take a line $L\subseteq M(A)$ when $M(A)
e0$, write $A=A_L\cdot(A_L^{-1}A)$ with $\dim M(A_L^{-1}A)=\dim M(A)-1$ by (4), and induct on $\dim M(A)$. For the prefix description, concatenate shortest factorizations of $B$ and of $B^{-1}A$ when $B\le_{\mathrm O}A$, and conversely read $A=B\cdot(B^{-1}A)$ with rank additivity. No Choice is used.
items.proof_strategy: direct computation of the kernel of A - A_U and of the restricted Wall form, with orthogonal projections and the finite-dimensional isometry characterization; induction on dim M(A) for the rank-length equality

items.statement:
Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system of finite type with $S$ finite, with $V=\mathbb R^S$, positive definite Coxeter form $B$, canonical reflection representation $\rho$, root system $\Phi$ and reflection set $T$ ([[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]], [[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]], [[thm-cg-finite-type-positive-definite-criterion]]), with the chamber system $wC$, the open faces $wC_I$ and the root hyperplanes $H_\alpha=\{x\in V:B(x,\alpha)=0\}$ of the transferred dual action ([[def-cg-finite-reflection-arrangement-and-spherical-chambers]]), and let $\ell_T$, $M$, $F$ and $\le_{\mathrm O}$ be as in [[def-cg-reflection-length-absolute-order-and-moved-space]]; for $u\in W$ write $M(u)=M(\rho(u))$ and $F(u)=F(\rho(u))$. Then:

**(1) Root normals in the moved space.** Let $w\in W$ with $w\ne1$. Then $\dim M(w)>0$ and there is a root $\alpha\in\Phi$ with $F(w)\subseteq H_\alpha$. For every such root one has $\alpha\in M(w)$, and the reflection $t_\alpha\in T$ with $\rho(t_\alpha)=r_\alpha$ ([[thm-cg-root-inversion-formulas-and-strong-exchange]] (1), [[lem-cg-reflection-form-invariance-and-rank-two-orders]] (2)) satisfies

$$\rho(t_\alpha)\le_{\mathrm O}\rho(w),\qquad \dim M(w)=1+\dim M(t_\alpha w).$$

**(2) Factorizations and Carter's formula.** Every $w\in W$ is a product $w=t_1t_2\cdots t_k$ of $k=\dim M(w)$ reflections $t_i\in T$, and no product of fewer elements of $T$ represents $w$; equivalently

$$\ell_T(w)=\dim M(w).$$

**(3) Independent normals.** Let $t_1,\dots,t_m\in T$ and choose roots $\alpha_i\in\Phi$ with $\rho(t_i)=r_{\alpha_i}$. Then $\dim M(t_1\cdots t_m)\le m$; and if $\dim M(t_1\cdots t_m)=m$ — in particular if $t_1\cdots t_m$ is a shortest reflection factorization of its product — then the $m$ vectors

$$\alpha_1,\ \rho(t_1)\alpha_2,\ \rho(t_1t_2)\alpha_3,\ \dots,\ \rho(t_1t_2\cdots t_{m-1})\alpha_m$$

are linearly independent ([[def-linear-independence]]) and span $M(t_1\cdots t_m)$.

items.title: Carter's reflection-length formula, the absolute order on a finite Coxeter group, and moved-space rigidity under a common upper bound

references.locator: Introduction and section 2 (printed pp. 1-3: reflection length, absolute order, moved and fixed spaces M(A), F(A), M(A)=F(A)^perp, the main result of [7], and notes (1)-(7)); the opening of section 3 through Note 3.5 (printed pp. 3-6); and the opening paragraphs of section 4 (printed pp. 8-9) with the A_3 intersection example

items.statement:
Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system of finite type with $S$ finite, with $V=\mathbb R^S$, positive definite Coxeter form $B$, canonical reflection representation $\rho$, root system $\Phi$, reflection set $T$ and length function $\ell$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]], [[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]], [[thm-cg-finite-type-positive-definite-criterion]]), and let $\ell_T$, $M$, $F$ and $\le_T$ be as in [[def-cg-reflection-length-absolute-order-and-moved-space]]. Then:

**(1) Carter's formula.** For every $w\in W$,

$$\ell_T(w)=\dim M(w)=\dim V-\dim F(w).$$

**(2) The absolute order.** $\le_T$ is a partial order on $W$ ([[def-partial-order]]), and:

**(i)** $u\le_T v$ holds if and only if there are reflections $t_1,\dots,t_m\in T$ and an index $k\le m$ such that $u=t_1\cdots t_k$ and $v=t_1\cdots t_m$ are shortest reflection factorizations, that is, $k=\ell_T(u)$ and $m=\ell_T(v)$ (a shortest reflection factorization of $u$ is a prefix of one of $v$);

**(ii)** $\ell_T(1)=0$, $u<_T v$ implies $\ell_T(u)<\ell_T(v)$, and $\ell_T(y)=\ell_T(x)+1$ whenever $y$ covers $x$; hence $\ell_T$ is a rank function and every interval $[u,v]_T=\{x\in W:u\le_Tx\le_Tv\}$ is finite ([[def-graded-poset-and-rank]]);

**(iii)** $|\ell_T(u)-\ell_T(v)|\le\ell_T(u^{-1}v)$, $\ell_T(u^{-1})=\ell_T(u)$ and $\ell_T(vuv^{-1})=\ell_T(u)$ for all $u,v\in W$;

**(iv)** $u\le_T v$ implies $M(u)\subseteq M(v)$ and $F(v)\subseteq F(u)$.

**(3) Moved-space rigidity under a common upper bound.** Let $\alpha,\beta,\delta\in W$ with $\alpha\le_T\delta$ and $\beta\le_T\delta$. Then

$$\alpha\le_T\beta\iff M(\alpha)\subseteq M(\beta);$$

in particular $M(\alpha)=M(\beta)$ implies $\alpha=\beta$, and $u\mapsto M(u)$ is an order isomorphism from $[1,\delta]_T$ onto its image ordered by inclusion. The proof of the converse uses the common upper bound $\delta$, through the restriction of $\delta$ to the subspace $M(\alpha)$; the converse is claimed only under this hypothesis (see the companion example of the $I_2(4)$ rotation, where the hypothesis fails).
items.strategy: *(1)* Immediate from the factorization lemma (2), which gives both $\ell_T(w)=\dim M(w)$ inside $W$; the second equality is $V=M(w)\oplus F(w)$ from the restriction lemma (1). *(2) Partial order.* Reflexivity is $\ell_T(u)=\ell_T(u)+\ell_T(1)$ with $\ell_T(1)=0$; antisymmetry follows from $u\le_Tv\le_Tu$ by the triangle inequality and $\ell_T(x)=0\Rightarrow x=1$; transitivity follows from $\ell_T(w)\le\ell_T(u)+\ell_T(u^{-1}w)\le\ell_T(u)+\ell_T(u^{-1}v)+\ell_T(v^{-1}w)=\ell_T(w)$, in which both inequalities must be equalities. For a cover $x<_T y$ the difference $\ell_T(y)-\ell_T(x)=\ell_T(x^{-1}y)$ is one: if it were $k\ge2$, splitting a shortest factorization of $x^{-1}y$ at one reflection would produce an element strictly between $x$ and $y$ by the prefix form (i), contradiction. So $\ell_T$ is a rank function, and finiteness of $W$ makes every interval finite. Part (i) is proved by concatenating shortest factorizations of $u$ and of $u^{-1}v$ in one direction, and by reading $v=u\cdot(u^{-1}v)$ with rank additivity in the other. Part (iii) is the triangle inequality for $u^{-1}v$, together with the facts that $T$ is closed under inversion and conjugation: $M(vuv^{-1})=\rho(v)M(u)$ has the same dimension as $M(u)$. Part (iv) is the first clause of the restriction lemma (4) applied to $B=\rho(u)$, $A=\rho(v)$ after translating the length comparison into the dimension comparison via (1). *(3)* Since $\ell_T=\dim M$ on $W$, the relation $\le_T$ coincides on $W$ with the orthogonal relation $\le_{\mathrm O}$; hence $\alpha,\beta\le_{\mathrm O}\delta$. If $M(\alpha)\subseteq M(\beta)$, then by the restriction lemma (4) applied to $A=\delta$ the elements $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the restrictions of $\delta$ to their moved spaces, and composing the displayed formula of restriction lemma (3) with $\Pi_{M(\alpha)}\Pi_{M(\beta)}=\Pi_{M(\alpha)}$ gives $(\beta)_{M(\alpha)}=\delta_{M(\alpha)}=\alpha$, so $\alpha\le_{\mathrm O}\beta$ and hence $\alpha\le_T\beta$. Conversely if $\alpha\le_T\beta$ the same translation and the restriction lemma give $M(\alpha)\subseteq M(\beta)$. The common upper bound is used exactly at the two applications of the restriction lemma to $\delta$; no unconditional converse is asserted, and the companion example of the $I_2(4)$ rotation shows that it fails when no common upper bound exists. No Choice is used.
items.proof_strategy: assembly of the factorization lemma and the restriction lemma: triangle inequality and rank addition for the partial order, and restriction of the common upper bound to moved subspaces for the rigidity

title: Finite Reflection Length and Orthogonal Moved Spaces — Examples

items.title: Simple and reflection lengths of a long transposition in $S_5$

references.title: R. W. Carter, Conjugacy classes in the Weyl group, Compositio Mathematica 25 (1972) 1-59 (Numdam full text)
references.locator: Section 2 'Products of reflections', printed pp. 2-5: the root-system setup (i)-(iv) and Lemmas 1-5 with the proofs of Lemmas 2, 3 and 4

references.title: A. Bjorner and F. Brenti, Combinatorics of Coxeter Groups, Springer GTM 231 (2005), author/class-hosted complete PDF
references.locator: Chapter 2, Exercise 2.35 on printed p. 61 (absolute length a-l(w)=min{k: w=t_1...t_k, t_i in T}); Chapter 7, Exercise 2 on printed pp. 234-235

items.statement:
Let $W$ be the Coxeter group of type $A_4$, with $S=\{s_1,\dots,s_4\}$, reflection representation $V=\mathbb R^S$ with positive definite Coxeter form $B$, reflection set $T$ and lengths $\ell$ and $\ell_T$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]], [[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]], [[def-cg-reflection-length-absolute-order-and-moved-space]], [[thm-cg-carter-reflection-length-and-absolute-order]]); fix the isomorphism $\varphi:W\to S_5$ with $s_i\mapsto(i\ i+1)$ ([[def-cg-coxeter-diagram-components-and-finite-type]], [[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (4), [[def-inversions-inversion-number-and-sign]]). Then:

**(i)** $T=\{\varphi^{-1}(\tau):\tau\text{ a transposition of }S_5\}$ and $\ell_T(w)=1$ for the transpositions $w$; for a transposition $(i\ j)$ with $i<j$ one has $\ell(\varphi^{-1}(i\ j))=2(j-i)-1$.

**(ii)** For the long transposition $\varphi^{-1}(1\ 5)$ the two lengths are $\ell=2\cdot4-1=7$ while $\ell_T=1$; explicitly $(1\ 5)=(2\ 5)(1\ 2)(2\ 5)^{-1}$ is a reflection and has $7$ inversions.

**(iii)** Under the linear isometry $e_{s_i}\mapsto\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(e_i-e_{i+1})$ of $(V,B)$ onto the hyperplane $\mathbf H=\{x\in\mathbb R^5:\sum_ix_i=0\}$ with the standard inner product ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]]), $\varphi$ corresponds to the permutation action, so $F(\varphi^{-1}(\sigma))$ corresponds to the fixed space $\{x\in\mathbf H:\sigma x=x\}$, of dimension $c(\sigma)-1$ for the cycle count $c(\sigma)$ (fixed points included). Since $\dim M=\dim V-\dim F$ ([[cor-double-orthogonal-complement-and-dimension]]) and $\ell_T=\dim M$, one has $\ell_T(\varphi^{-1}(\sigma))=\dim\mathbf H-(c(\sigma)-1)=5-c(\sigma)$ for every $\sigma\in S_5$. In particular $\ell_T(\varphi^{-1}(1\ 5))=1$; for the longest element $w_0=\varphi^{-1}((1\ 5)(2\ 4))$ one has $\ell(w_0)=10$ while $\ell_T(w_0)=5-3=2$ (the reversal has three cycles), and every $5$-cycle has $\ell_T=4=\dim V$.
items.strategy: The verification is finite and explicit. The transpositions generate $S_5$ as conjugates of the adjacent transpositions: $\varphi(s_i)=(i\ i+1)$ and $\sigma(i\ i+1)\sigma^{-1}=(\sigma(i)\ \sigma(i+1))$, while $(i\ j)$ is conjugated to $(1\ 2)$ by the permutation swapping $1\leftrightarrow i$, $2\leftrightarrow j$; by the definition $T=\{wsw^{-1}\}$, the transpositions are exactly the elements $t_\alpha$ and unit transpositional form gives (i) and (ii). The length formula in (i) is the inversion count of a transposition, from [[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (4): the pairs $(i,k)$, $i<k<j$, and $(k,j)$, $i<k<j$, together with $(i,j)$, are exactly $2(j-i)-1$ inversions, and $(1\ 5)$ has the seven inversions $\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{1,4\},\{1,5\},\{2,5\},\{3,5\},\{4,5\}$. In (iii), the four vectors $(e_i-e_{i+1})/\sqrt2$ satisfy $B(e_{s_i},e_{s_j})=-\cos(\pi/3)=-\tfrac12$ for adjacent indices and $0$ otherwise, matching the standard inner products, and they span the four-dimensional space $\mathbf H$; the conjugation rule of [[lem-cg-reflection-representation-descends-and-root-norms]] (4) identifies $\rho$ with the permutation action on $\mathbf H$. A permutation matrix has eigenvalue $1$ exactly on the vectors constant on each cycle, so $F$ has dimension $c(\sigma)-1$; the dimension formula and [[thm-cg-carter-reflection-length-and-absolute-order]] (1) give $\ell_T=5-c(\sigma)$. For the reversal $(1\ 5)(2\ 4)$ the inversion number is $10$ and $c=3$, so $\ell_T=2$; a $5$-cycle has $c=1$ and $\ell_T=4$.
items.proof_strategy: explicit type-A computation: transposition conjugacy for T, inversion counts for the simple length, and the isometry of the reflection representation with the sum-zero hyperplane for the fixed-space dimension

items.title: The Wall form and line restrictions of a plane rotation, and the necessity of a common upper bound

references.title: T. Brady and C. Watt, Lattices in finite real reflection groups (arXiv:math/0501502)
references.locator: Introduction and section 2 (printed pp. 1-3: reflection length, absolute order, moved and fixed spaces M(A), F(A), M(A)=F(A)^perp, the main result of [7], and notes (1)-(7)); the opening of section 3 through Note 3.5 (printed pp. 3-6); and the opening paragraphs of section 4 (printed pp. 8-9) with the A_3 intersection example

references.title: R. W. Carter, Conjugacy classes in the Weyl group, Compositio Mathematica 25 (1972) 1-59 (Numdam full text)
references.locator: Section 2 'Products of reflections', printed pp. 2-5: the root-system setup (i)-(iv) and Lemmas 1-5 with the proofs of Lemmas 2, 3 and 4

items.statement:
Let $m\ge3$, $c=\cos(\pi/m)$, $V=\mathbb Re_s+\mathbb Re_t$ with the positive definite Coxeter form $B$ of the rank-two system $I_2(m)$, and let $A:=\rho(st)=r_sr_t$ ([[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]], [[lem-cg-reflection-form-invariance-and-rank-two-orders]] (3), [[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]], [[thm-cg-finite-coxeter-classification-including-h-and-dihedral]]); let $\ell_T$, $M$ and $\le_{\mathrm O}$ be as in [[def-cg-reflection-length-absolute-order-and-moved-space]] and [[lem-cg-orthogonal-wall-form-and-subspace-restriction]], and let $T$, $\Phi$ be the reflection set and root system ([[thm-cg-root-inversion-formulas-and-strong-exchange]] (1)). Use faithfulness of [[thm-cg-root-length-criterion-and-faithfulness]] (3) to identify $W$ with $\rho(W)$ when writing $\ell$, $\ell_T$ and $\le_T$ for these operators. Then:

**(i)** $\operatorname{tr}A=2\cos(2\pi/m)\ne2=\operatorname{tr}\mathrm{id}$, so $1$ is not an eigenvalue of $A$, $F(A)=0$ and $M(A)=V$. In oriented orthonormal coordinates adapted to $A$ it is the rotation by $\theta=2\pi/m$, and

$$S_A=(A-\mathrm{id})^{-1}\ \text{is multiplication by}\ \frac{1}{e^{i\theta}-1}=-\frac12-\frac i2\cot\frac\theta2,$$

so the Wall form $\chi_A(u,v)=B(S_Au,v)$ satisfies $\chi_A(u,v)+\chi_A(v,u)=-B(u,v)$ with symmetric part $-\frac12B$.

**(ii)** For every line $L\subseteq V$ the operator $H_L=\Pi_LS_A\Pi_L$ is the scalar $-\frac12$ on $L$, so $A_L=\mathrm{id}-2\Pi_L$ is the reflection of the plane with normal line $L$, $A_L\le_{\mathrm O}A$, and $L\mapsto A_L$ is a bijection from the lines of $V$ onto the reflections $B\le_{\mathrm O}A$. Moreover $A_L$ lies in $\rho(W)$ if and only if $L$ is one of the $m$ root lines $\mathbb R\beta$, $\beta\in\Phi$; so for a line $L$ that is not a root line, $A_L$ is an orthogonal reflection whose moved space is $L$ but $A_L\notin\rho(W)$.

**(iii)** Take $m=4$ and put $w_0:=A^2$ (the rotation by $\pi$, the longest element of $W=I_2(4)$). Then $M(A)=M(w_0)=V$, so $M(w_0)\subseteq M(A)$, while

$$\ell_T(w_0^{-1}A)=\ell_T(A^{-1}w_0)=\ell_T(A)=2,$$

so $w_0\not\le_T A$ and $A\not\le_T w_0$; in fact $A$ and $w_0$ have no common upper bound in $W$, since every $\delta\in W$ has $\ell_T(\delta)=\dim M(\delta)\le2$ ([[thm-cg-carter-reflection-length-and-absolute-order]] (1)), so a common upper bound would have to equal both $A$ and $w_0$. Hence the implication $M(\alpha)\subseteq M(\beta)\Rightarrow\alpha\le_T\beta$ fails without the common-upper-bound hypothesis of the rigidity theorem.
items.strategy: *(i)* By [[lem-cg-reflection-form-invariance-and-rank-two-orders]] (3)(iv) the product $r_sr_t$ has trace $2\cos(2\pi/m)$ and determinant $1$, so it is the rotation by $\pm2\pi/m$ in the positive definite plane, and $1$ is not an eigenvalue for $m\ge3$. $S_A=\frac1{e^{i\theta}-1}$ is computed from $e^{i\theta}-1=e^{i\theta/2}(e^{i\theta/2}-e^{-i\theta/2})=2ie^{i\theta/2}\sin(\theta/2)$; since $F(A)=0$ and $M(A)=V$, the restriction lemma (2) gives the identity for $\chi_A$ directly. *(ii)* $H_L$ is a $1\times1$ operator with $H_L+H_L^*=-1$, hence the real scalar $-\frac12$ (by the definition of $H_L$ and the restriction lemma (2)); the description of $A_L$ and the bijection with reflections $\le_{\mathrm O}A$ are restriction lemma (3) and (5). The reflection $A_L$ lies in $\rho(W)$ iff $A_L=\rho(w)$ for some $w\in W$; then $\dim M(w)=1$, so the root-existence clause in [[lem-cg-reflection-factorizations-and-independent-normals]] (1) supplies a root $\alpha\in M(w)$, whence $M(w)=\mathbb R\alpha$, $\rho(w)=r_\alpha=\rho(t_\alpha)$ and $w=t_\alpha$ by faithfulness [[thm-cg-root-length-criterion-and-faithfulness]] (3). Hence only the $m$ root lines $\mathbb R\beta$, $\beta\in\Phi$, occur. *(iii)* Because $A$ is the rotation by $\pi/2$, $A^2$ is the rotation by $\pi$, so $A^2=-\mathrm{id}$ and $M(A^2)=V=M(A)$. In $I_2(4)$ the eight elements are $A^k$ and $A^ks$ with $0\le k\le3$; by $\ell_T=\dim M$ ([[thm-cg-carter-reflection-length-and-absolute-order]] (1)) and $M(A^ks)=\mathbb R\alpha$ one has $\ell_T(A^ks)=1$, while $\ell_T(A)=\ell_T(A^3)=\ell_T(A^2)=2$ and $\ell_T(1)=0$. Hence $\ell_T(w_0^{-1}A)=\ell_T(A^2A)=\ell_T(A^3)=2$ and $\ell_T(A^{-1}w_0)=\ell_T(A^3A^2)=\ell_T(A)=2$, so both inequalities $2\le2+2$ fail. Finally $\dim M(\delta)\le\dim V=2$ for every $\delta$, so a common upper bound $\delta$ of $A$ and $w_0$ would satisfy $2=\ell_T(A)\le\ell_T(\delta)\le2$ and $\ell_T(\delta)=\ell_T(A)+\ell_T(A^{-1}\delta)$, forcing $\delta=A$, which is not above $w_0$; so no common upper bound exists. No Choice is used.
items.proof_strategy: explicit two-dimensional rotation computation of the Wall form and its line restrictions in the dihedral model, with the I2(4) pair A and A^2 as a witness that the common-upper-bound hypothesis is needed

items.title: A moved-space intersection in $A_3$ that is not the meet

references.title: T. Brady and C. Watt, Lattices in finite real reflection groups (arXiv:math/0501502)
references.locator: Introduction and section 2 (printed pp. 1-3: reflection length, absolute order, moved and fixed spaces M(A), F(A), M(A)=F(A)^perp, the main result of [7], and notes (1)-(7)); the opening of section 3 through Note 3.5 (printed pp. 3-6); and the opening paragraphs of section 4 (printed pp. 8-9) with the A_3 intersection example

references.title: R. W. Carter, Conjugacy classes in the Weyl group, Compositio Mathematica 25 (1972) 1-59 (Numdam full text)
references.locator: Section 2 'Products of reflections', printed pp. 2-5: the root-system setup (i)-(iv) and Lemmas 1-5 with the proofs of Lemmas 2, 3 and 4

items.statement:
Let $W$ be the Coxeter group of type $A_3$, with $S=\{s_1,s_2,s_3\}$, $V=\mathbb R^S$ with positive definite Coxeter form, reflection set $T$ and lengths $\ell_T,\ell$, and let $\varphi:W\to S_4$, $s_i\mapsto(i\ i+1)$, be the type-A isomorphism ([[def-cg-coxeter-diagram-components-and-finite-type]], [[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]], [[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]], [[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (4), [[def-cg-reflection-length-absolute-order-and-moved-space]], [[thm-cg-carter-reflection-length-and-absolute-order]]). Put

$$\gamma=\varphi^{-1}(1\,2\,3\,4),\quad \alpha=\varphi^{-1}\bigl((1\,2)(3\,4)\bigr),\quad \beta=\varphi^{-1}\bigl((1\,4)(2\,3)\bigr).$$

Then:

**(i)** $\ell_T(\gamma)=3$, $\ell_T(\alpha)=\ell_T(\beta)=2$, and $\alpha\le_T\gamma$, $\beta\le_T\gamma$: indeed $\alpha\gamma=\varphi^{-1}(2\ 4)$ and $\beta\gamma=\varphi^{-1}(1\ 3)$ are reflections, so $\gamma=\alpha\cdot\alpha^{-1}\gamma$ and $\gamma=\beta\cdot\beta^{-1}\gamma$ display the rank additivity $3=2+1$.

**(ii)** Under the isometry $e_{s_i}\mapsto\frac1{\sqrt2}(e_i-e_{i+1})$ of $V$ with $\mathbf H=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:\sum_ix_i=0\}$ and the standard inner product, one has

$$M(\alpha)=\{x\in\mathbf H:x_2=-x_1,\ x_4=-x_3\},\qquad M(\beta)=\{x\in\mathbf H:x_2=-x_3,\ x_4=-x_1\},$$

and $M(\alpha)\cap M(\beta)=\mathbb R(e_1-e_2+e_3-e_4)$ is a line containing no root of $A_3$.

**(iii)** No element of $W$ has moved space $M(\alpha)\cap M(\beta)$: a nonzero moved space of an element of $W$ contains a root ([[lem-cg-reflection-factorizations-and-independent-normals]] (1)), while this line contains none. Moreover the greatest common lower bound of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ in $(W,\le_T)$ is $1$: any common lower bound $\tau$ satisfies $M(\tau)\subseteq M(\alpha)\cap M(\beta)$ ([[thm-cg-carter-reflection-length-and-absolute-order]] (2)(iv)), so $\tau=1$ by the same root-existence clause; hence the moved space of the meet, $M(1)=0$, is strictly smaller than the intersection of the two moved spaces, and arbitrary subspace intersection does not compute the meet.
items.strategy: All computations are explicit; permutation products are computed with the standard convention $(\sigma\tau)(x)=\sigma(\tau(x))$. *(i)* In the type A reflection representation the reflections act as transpositions under $\varphi$; a 4-cycle has $c=1$, so $\ell_T=\dim M=4-1=3$ and its fixed space is $0$, while $(1\,2)(3\,4)$ and $(1\,4)(2\,3)$ have $c=2$ and $\ell_T=\dim M=3-(2-1)=2$ (calculating fixed spaces as in the companion example of the long transposition, or directly below); the products $\alpha\gamma=(1\,2)(3\,4)\cdot(1\,2\,3\,4)=(2\,4)$ and $\beta\gamma=(1\,4)(2\,3)\cdot(1\,2\,3\,4)=(1\,3)$ are computed by one-line multiplication, and both are transpositions, i.e. elements of $T$. *(ii)* The fixed space of $(1\,2)(3\,4)$ on $\mathbf H$ is spanned by $e_1+e_2-e_3-e_4$, whose orthogonal complement in $\mathbf H$ is spanned by $e_1-e_2$ and $e_3-e_4$; the fixed space of $(1\,4)(2\,3)$ is spanned by $e_1-e_2-e_3+e_4$ with orthogonal complement in $\mathbf H$ spanned by $e_1-e_4$ and $e_2-e_3$; intersecting the two two-dimensional moved spaces gives $x_2=-x_1$, $x_3=x_1$, $x_4=-x_1$, i.e. the displayed line, and the normalized roots of $A_3$ are the $\pm(e_i-e_j)/\sqrt2$, none of which is a multiple of $e_1-e_2+e_3-e_4$. *(iii)* Apply the root-existence clause of [[lem-cg-reflection-factorizations-and-independent-normals]] (1) to any nonzero $\tau\le_T\alpha$, and the inclusion $\tau\le_T\alpha\Rightarrow M(\tau)\subseteq M(\alpha)$ of [[thm-cg-carter-reflection-length-and-absolute-order]] (2)(iv). The common upper bound $\gamma$ is present but is not needed for this conclusion; the point of the example is that the correct meet is strictly smaller than the subspace intersection.
items.proof_strategy: explicit A3 computation of two moved spaces, their one-dimensional non-root intersection and the absence of a non-identity common lower bound
